limitations_and_boundaries: The analysis focuses on long-range problems; short-range tasks may not suffer from over-squashing.
The FA layer solution is simple and may not be optimal; better solutions may exist.
Theoretical bounds are derived for a specific synthetic problem (TREE-NEIGHBORSMATCH) and may not directly transfer to all real-world graphs.
Over-squashing is distinct from over-smoothing; the paper does not fully disentangle their interaction in all scenarios.
The FA layer adds O(N^2) edges, which may be computationally expensive for very large graphs.

missed_core_items.description: The paper mentions that the FA layer is added only in the last layer, and the first K-1 layers use the original sparse topology. This is a core methodological detail.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: converting an existing layer to be fully-adjacent means that Nv := V for every node v ∈V, in that layer only. This does not change the type of layer nor add weights, but only changes adjacency of a data sample in a single layer. Thus, the K −1 graph layers exploit the graph structure using their original sparse topology, and only the K-th layer is an FA layer

missed_core_items.description: The paper reports that the average diameter of QM9 graphs is 6.35±0.91, max 10, 90th percentile 8, and that models with 10 layers did not improve, indicating that the improvement from FA is due to reducing over-squashing, not under-reaching.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: we measured the graphs’ diameter in the QM9 dataset – the maximum shortest path between any two nodes in a graph. We found that the average diameter is 6.35±0.91, the maximum diameter is 10, and the 90’th percentile is 8, while most models were trained with K=8 layers. That is, at least 90% of the examples in the dataset certainly did not suffer from under-reaching, because the number of layers was greater or equal than their diameter. We trained another set of models with 10 layers, which did not show an improvement over the base models. We conclude that the source of improvement was clearly not the increased reachability, but instead, the reduction in over-squashing.

missed_core_items.description: The paper reports that doubling the hidden dimension size (2×d) led to only 5.5% improvement, while FA layer achieved 42% improvement, showing that increasing dimension is ineffective.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: 2×d is a model that was trained with a doubled hidden dimension size, d = 256 instead of d = 128 as in the base model. As shown, doubling the hidden dimension size leads to a small improvement of only 5.5% reduction in error. In comparison, the +FA model used the original dimension sizes and achieves a much larger improvement of 43.40%.

missed_core_items.description: The paper reports that using all layers as FA (ignoring graph topology) led to 1500% higher error, showing that graph structure is still important.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: All FA is a model that was trained with all GNN layers converted into FA layers, practically ignoring the graph topology. This led to much worse results of more than 1500% higher error.

missed_core_items.description: The paper reports that using only a fraction of edges in the FA layer (partial FA) still reduces error, e.g., 0.5× FA reduces error by 31.5%.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: using only half of the edges (0.5× FA) reduces the error by 31.5%.

missed_core_items.description: The paper reports that the penultimate FA layer (FA as the K-1-th layer) led to slightly better results than +FA.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: Penultimate FA is a model where the FA layer is the penultimate layer (the K −1-th), followed by a standard GNN layer as the K-th layer. This led to results that are even slightly better than +FA.

missed_core_items.description: The paper reports that in the TREE-NEIGHBORSMATCH experiment, when the long-range is maintained but the amount of information is reduced (chain setting), all GNNs easily fit the data, showing that over-squashing, not long-range itself, is the problem.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: we repeated the experiment of Figure 3 for depths 4 to 8, where the distance between the leaves and the target node remained the same, but the amount of over-squashing was as in r=2. That is, the graph looks like a tree of depth=2, where the root is connected to a “chain” of length of up to 6, and the target node is at the other side of the chain. This setting maintains the long-range as in the original problem, but reduces the amount of information that needs to be squashed. In other words, This setting disentangles of the effect of the long-range itself from the effect of the growing amount of information (i.e., from over-squashing). In this setting, all GNN types managed to easily fit the data to close to 100% across all distances, showing that the problem is the amount of over-squashing, rather than the long-range itself.
